newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala aghast at U.S. shackling of deportees.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala aghast at U.S. shackling of deportees.

text.p: Guatemala on Thursday called on the United States to treat deported illegal immigrants humanely after 56 deportees arrived home in shackles this week.

"The position of the Guatemalan government is that that the human rights of immigrants should be protected, regardless of their immigration status," Foreign Minister Eduardo Stein said in a statement.
Four of the 56 deported men were wanted by the police for crimes in Guatemala and were arrested upon their arrival, officials said.

Guatemalan immigration director Edgar Montes said he thought U.S. authorities had made an error in shackling the men, who arrived Monday evening on a chartered flight from Houston. The men were handcuffed during the whole flight. Most deportees are not sent back in chains.

"We are asking for an explanation from the United States director of immigration for the procedure employed with the deported men who arrived in the national territory in chains," Montes said in a news release.

Since April 1 when major portions of a new U.S. law went into effect accelerating the process for deporting illegal immigrants, Guatemala and other Central American nations have feared that a flood of deportations would put pressure on local job markets and harm fragile economies.
At a regional summit in May in Costa Rica U.S. President Bill Clinton promised his Central American counterparts there would not be massive deportations.
According to Montes there has been a slight increase in the number of deportations to Guatemala in the first six months of 1997 compared to the same period in 1996. He did not have exact figures.
Though the feared flood of deportations has not materialised, Guatemalans were aghast at news photos of the shackled deportees. Government officials joined the outcry.

"Our country's official position is that undocumented immigrants who go to developed nations should not be considered criminals since their motivation is not to break the law but to have access to jobs," said Stein, the foreign minister.
President Alvaro Arzu said he would meet with the U.S. ambassador in Guatemala to seek his point of view on the case.
"First we need to know the reasons for the deportations and await an explanation of why these people returned in shackles," Arzu said in a news release.
